items.title: Recording a finance transaction
items.question: How do I record a finance transaction?
alternatives: how do I enter a milk sale
items.answer: Enter the actual transaction type, amount, date, governed category, payment method, counterparty and operator attribution, then verify the persisted ledger record before relying on any report.
items.explanation: DairyOS classifies a transaction by its type. INCOME and RECEIPT are revenue; EXPENSE and PAYMENT are expenses; OWNER_INVESTMENT is a capital inflow; OWNER_WITHDRAWAL and LOAN_PAYMENT are cash movements rather than trading results. That distinction is why an owner drawing money out does not appear as an expense and does not reduce profit. Revenue carries its own governed categories: milk sales, manure, six animal sale categories covering milking animal, dry animal, heifer, female calf, male calf and bull, and other revenue.

scenario.given: A fictional farm records a purchase of veterinary supplies.
steps: Open Finance.
Select the governed transaction type and category.
Enter amount, date, counterparty, payment facts and notes.
Save once and verify the ledger result.
scenario.expected: One attributable active financial fact is persisted and classified, with a status of RECORDED unless a settlement state was chosen.
scenario.next: Review its payment status, category totals and the relevant cost views.

persisted: the transaction with its type, amount, date, category and counterparty
derived: transaction nature of revenue, expense, capital inflow or cash movement

exceptions.condition: The entry does not fit a governed category.
exceptions.behaviour: Escalate for finance review. Do not invent a category spelling that bypasses the taxonomy.

exceptions.condition: An owner puts money in or takes money out.
exceptions.behaviour: That is a capital inflow or a cash movement, not revenue or expense, and does not affect trading results.

items.correction_path: Amend through the governed edit path, or void the transaction if it should not exist. Never edit the ledger outside the API.
items.safety: Do not use a generic adjustment to conceal an unclassified source transaction.

perspectives.operator: Enter what the document says, with the category that matches what was actually bought or sold.
perspectives.supervisor: An uncategorised or miscategorised entry distorts cost reporting silently.
perspectives.finance: Type drives nature: only INCOME and RECEIPT are revenue, only EXPENSE and PAYMENT are expenses.
perspectives.veterinary_health: A veterinary invoice is a finance transaction; the clinical record is separate.
perspectives.technical: transaction_classifier resolves nature from the transaction type and active status.
perspectives.training: Classify a fictional owner withdrawal and confirm it is not an expense.
perspectives.troubleshooting: If a figure is missing from a total, check the transaction's type and its active status first.

items.title: Choosing an expense category
items.question: Which category should I use for an expense?
items.answer: Use the governed taxonomy. Every expense is entered under one of three master categories, Feed, OPEX or Non-OPEX, then a group within it, then a specific item.
items.explanation: The taxonomy has exactly three master categories. Feed covers green fodder and silage, dry roughages, commercial feeds and grains, protein meals and cakes, minerals and premixes. OPEX covers ten groups including veterinary and herd health, breeding and reproduction, labour and salaries, utilities, machinery, dairy chemicals, bedding, logistics and admin, and land and rent. Non-OPEX contains only two items in total: Animal Purchase and Equipment Purchase. Categorisation matters because the category decides which attribution rule applies and whether the cost can reach cost of production at all. TMR ingredients must use the shared TMR catalogue identity so that Finance and Feed stay aligned on the same ingredient.

scenario.given: A fictional farm buys semen straws.
steps: Identify the economic substance of the expense.
Choose the master category, then the group, then the item.
For TMR inputs, select the matching governed ingredient.
Save and verify the category totals.
scenario.expected: The expense is recorded under OPEX, in the Breeding and Reproduction group, as the item Semen Straws, and becomes available to the consumption attribution rule.
scenario.next: Review the attribution method and whether the item reaches cost of production.

persisted: master category, group and item on the transaction

exceptions.condition: The item is Other, Small Tools and Implements, Building or Yard Repairs, or Taxes and Local Fees.
exceptions.behaviour: These have no default cost classification. The operator must decide per transaction whether it is OPEX or Non-OPEX.

exceptions.condition: The expense is a TMR ingredient.
exceptions.behaviour: It must use the shared TMR catalogue identity, or Feed and Finance will disagree about the same ingredient.

items.correction_path: Amend the transaction through the governed edit path. The original category remains in the audit trail.
items.safety: Do not create category spellings that bypass the governed taxonomy; an unrecognised item has no attribution rule.

perspectives.operator: Pick the item that names what you actually bought.
perspectives.supervisor: Four items deliberately have no default classification and need a judgement each time.
perspectives.finance: The category drives both the cost classification and the attribution method.
perspectives.veterinary_health: Veterinary and breeding consumables are OPEX groups, not capital.
perspectives.technical: EXPENSE_TAXONOMIES holds FEED, OPEX and NON_OPEX; NON_OPEX contains only Animal Purchase and Equipment Purchase.
perspectives.training: Categorise a fictional tractor diesel purchase and note that its method is not automatic.
perspectives.troubleshooting: If a cost never appears in cost of production, check its item against the exclusions.

items.title: Payment status and settlement
items.question: How do I record whether a transaction was paid?
items.answer: Set the governed status from actual settlement evidence. The value incurred and the cash movement are distinct facts, and changing status never rewrites the original amount.
items.explanation: A transaction starts as RECORDED and may move to PAYABLE or RECEIVABLE. A payable settles to PAID; a receivable settles to RECEIVED. Every state can be voided. What is not possible is going back: once PAID or RECEIVED, the only remaining move is VOID. There is also no partial settlement anywhere in the model, so a transaction settles once and in full. RECORDED is treated as cash at the time of recording, which is why it is the right status for something paid immediately and the wrong status for something owed.

scenario.given: A fictional farm receives an invoice it will pay next month.
steps: Open the transaction.
Review the amount and counterparty.
Set the status to PAYABLE.
When it is actually settled, move it to PAID and verify the cash and ageing views.
scenario.expected: The liability is visible while outstanding, and settlement is recorded only once the payment actually happened. The original amount is unchanged throughout.
scenario.next: Follow any remaining outstanding items through the ageing view.

persisted: the status and its transition evidence
audit: each transition recorded against the transaction

exceptions.condition: Only part of an amount has been paid.
exceptions.behaviour: DairyOS has no partial settlement. A transaction settles once and in full, so a part payment must be handled as a matter of how the transactions were recorded.

exceptions.condition: A settled transaction turns out to be wrong.
exceptions.behaviour: PAID and RECEIVED cannot revert. The only onward transition is VOID.

exceptions.condition: The transaction was paid at the moment of recording.
exceptions.behaviour: RECORDED already represents cash at recording; it does not need to be moved to PAID.

items.correction_path: Void the transaction and record the correct one, since settled states cannot be reversed.
items.safety: Never mark something paid because it was entered or approved. Status must follow settlement evidence.

perspectives.operator: Change the status when the money actually moves, not when the paperwork does.
perspectives.supervisor: Marking items paid early makes the ageing view useless.
perspectives.finance: Incurred value and cash movement are separate; status carries the cash fact, the amount carries the value.
perspectives.technical: Transitions are constrained; settled statuses admit only VOID.
perspectives.training: Walk a fictional transaction from RECORDED to PAYABLE to PAID and try to reverse it.
perspectives.troubleshooting: If a status will not change, check the permitted transitions from its current state.

items.title: Correcting a finance entry
items.question: How do I correct a finance entry?
items.answer: Use the governed edit path with a reason. Dependent milk, feed, payroll and cost facts must stay synchronised with the correction.
items.explanation: A finance transaction is frequently the source of a derived figure elsewhere, so a correction has to carry through. Where a transaction is linked to another domain, such as a milk sale, the amendment applies across both or fails; a half-applied correction would leave production and revenue disagreeing with nothing to explain the gap. The prior value is retained, which is what lets a reviewer distinguish a genuine correction from a repeated error.

scenario.given: A fictional farm recorded an expense with the wrong amount.
steps: Locate the exact transaction.
Review its source document and the calculations that depend on it.
Submit the amendment with its reason.
Verify the ledger, the audit event and the downstream totals.
Recheck the affected cost or revenue period.
scenario.expected: The correction is attributable and every derived view reflects the corrected active fact.
scenario.next: Recheck the affected cost of production, OPEX, payable or revenue period.

persisted: the corrected values and the reason

exceptions.condition: A dependent fact in another domain cannot be synchronised.
exceptions.behaviour: The amendment fails rather than applying partially. Read the error.

exceptions.condition: The transaction should not exist at all.
exceptions.behaviour: Void it rather than amending it to zero.

items.correction_path: Amendments are themselves the correction path, each recorded with its reason.
items.safety: Do not edit database rows directly and do not create a compensating entry whose purpose is unexplained.

perspectives.operator: Say what the right figure is and why.
perspectives.supervisor: A compensating entry with no explanation is harder to audit than a correction.
perspectives.finance: Amending a linked transaction moves the dependent fact with it, or fails.
perspectives.technical: Amendment is atomic across linked domains.
perspectives.training: Amend a fictional linked sale and observe the atomicity.
perspectives.troubleshooting: A rejected amendment names the dependency that could not move.

items.title: Voiding a finance transaction
items.question: When should a finance transaction be voided, and what happens to it?
items.answer: Void an invalid or duplicate transaction through the governed status action. It is excluded from every active total while the original record and the reason are retained permanently.
items.explanation: Voiding is the one transition available from every state, including settled ones, and it requires a reason. The evidence is written into the transaction's notes as a stamped transition recording when it happened, what it moved from and to, and why. Three statuses mark a row inactive: VOID, CANCELLED and DELETED. None of them removes the row, which is the point. A period total that once reconciled stays explainable, and a reviewer can see both that the entry existed and that it was withdrawn.

scenario.given: A fictional farm finds a duplicate expense in the ledger.
steps: Review the source evidence and any dependencies.
Use the governed void action and give the reason.
Verify that active totals now exclude it.
Verify the original and its reason remain auditable.
scenario.expected: Active calculations are corrected without destructive deletion, and the transaction's notes carry a stamped record of the transition and its reason.
scenario.next: Enter a correct replacement only where the evidence supports one.

persisted: void status with its stamped reason in the notes
derived: active ledger totals that now exclude it

exceptions.condition: The transaction is already settled.
exceptions.behaviour: VOID is still available. It is the only transition out of PAID or RECEIVED.

exceptions.condition: The amount is merely wrong.
exceptions.behaviour: Amend it. Void is for a transaction that should not exist.

exceptions.condition: No reason is given.
exceptions.behaviour: The void is not accepted. The reason is the audit evidence.

items.correction_path: Record the correct replacement transaction. The voided one stays visible as history.
items.safety: Void is not deletion and must not be used to hide a control failure.

perspectives.operator: Use it for a duplicate or an entry that should never have been made, and say why.
perspectives.supervisor: Voids stay visible on purpose; a rising count is a control signal.
perspectives.finance: VOID, CANCELLED and DELETED all mark a row inactive; none removes it.
perspectives.technical: The transition stamp is appended to the transaction's notes as durable evidence.
perspectives.training: Void a fictional duplicate and find the stamped reason on the record.
perspectives.troubleshooting: If a total is lower than the ledger suggests, look for inactive rows before suspecting a fault.

items.title: Payroll
items.question: How does payroll enter DairyOS finance?
items.answer: Create and settle payroll through the governed payroll workflow, so that the payroll record and its corresponding financial and audit events are both retained.
items.explanation: Payroll is entered through its own workflow rather than as a free-form expense, because it carries an employee, a period and a liability that must remain linked to the resulting financial fact. Labour costs sit in the OPEX taxonomy under labour and salaries, covering milker wages, feeder and shed worker wages, supervisor and manager salary, daily labour, overtime, staff rations and payroll taxes. Those are periodic costs, so they attribute across the period they cover rather than landing entirely on the day they were paid.

scenario.given: A fictional farm runs monthly payroll for its milkers.
steps: Enter the payroll record with employee, period, amount and attribution.
Review the payable status.
Record payment through the governed action once settled.
Verify the Finance and audit history.
scenario.expected: The payroll liability, its payment state and its financial classification stay consistent with each other.
scenario.next: Review OPEX attribution for the period the payroll covers.

persisted: payroll record with employee, period and amount
projected: OPEX attributed across the covered period
audit: payroll register linked to the financial ledger

exceptions.condition: Payment has not actually been made.
exceptions.behaviour: Leave it payable. Settlement status follows evidence.

exceptions.condition: The payroll covers a period spanning a reporting boundary.
exceptions.behaviour: It attributes across its coverage dates, not to the payment date.

items.correction_path: Correct through the payroll workflow so the payroll record and the financial fact stay aligned.
items.safety: Do not mark payroll paid without settlement evidence.

perspectives.operator: Record the payroll for the period it covers.
perspectives.supervisor: Labour is usually the largest OPEX line; its period attribution matters.
perspectives.finance: Labour costs attribute periodically across their coverage dates.
perspectives.technical: Payroll has its own routes and remains linked to the resulting financial transaction.
perspectives.training: Enter a fictional payroll spanning two months and see how it attributes.
perspectives.troubleshooting: If labour cost lands in the wrong period, check the coverage dates rather than the payment date.

items.title: What counts as OPEX
items.question: Which expenses contribute to OPEX per litre, and why is an equipment purchase excluded?
alternatives: why isn't equipment purchase in OPEX
items.answer: Eligible operating expenses are attributed to the selected period by their governed rule and divided by the period's milk. Three items are classified Non-OPEX and never reach it: Equipment Purchase, Animal Purchase and Loan Interest.
items.explanation: There is a distinction here that is easy to miss, and it matters. An expense has an entry category and, separately, a cost-of-production classification. Loan Interest is entered under OPEX, in the logistics, admin and finance group, because that is where it belongs operationally. For cost of production it is classified Non-OPEX and excluded, alongside Equipment Purchase and Animal Purchase. All three are excluded for the same underlying reason: they are capital or financing costs rather than the operating cost of producing this period's milk. Including an equipment purchase would load a single period with an asset that serves many. Four further items have no default classification at all, namely Other, Small Tools and Implements, Building or Yard Repairs, and Taxes and Local Fees, so the operator decides for each transaction whether it is operating or capital in nature.

scenario.given: A fictional farm buys a milk chiller and pays its monthly electricity bill.
steps: Review the categories and active status of both transactions.
Inspect each one's attribution rule and period.
Compare the attributed OPEX with the period's milk denominator.
Investigate excluded or unattributed costs explicitly.
scenario.expected: The electricity attributes into the period as a periodic cost and contributes to OPEX per litre. The chiller is an Equipment Purchase, classified Non-OPEX, and is excluded from OPEX per litre entirely.
scenario.next: Review feed cost per litre separately, and combine the two only in cost of production per litre.

persisted: the classification chosen where the item has no default
audit: exclusions and unattributed amounts shown rather than hidden

exceptions.condition: The item is Equipment Purchase, Animal Purchase or Loan Interest.
exceptions.behaviour: Classified Non-OPEX and excluded from OPEX per litre, even though the first two are entered under Non-OPEX and the third under OPEX.

exceptions.condition: The item is one of the four with no default classification.
exceptions.behaviour: The operator must classify it for that transaction.

exceptions.condition: A cost cannot be attributed.
exceptions.behaviour: It is shown as unattributed rather than silently dropped or silently included.

items.correction_path: Correct the transaction's category or classification through the governed edit path; the attributed totals recompute.
items.safety: Do not silently include Non-OPEX or unattributed costs in an operating figure.

perspectives.operator: Buying a machine is not a running cost, so it does not appear in cost per litre.
perspectives.supervisor: The four unclassified items need a consistent house rule or reporting will drift.
perspectives.finance: Entry category and cost-of-production classification are different things; Loan Interest shows why.
perspectives.veterinary_health: Veterinary and breeding consumables are operating costs and do contribute.
perspectives.technical: default_cop_classification returns NON_OPEX for the three excluded items and None for the four conditional ones.
perspectives.training: Classify a fictional loan interest payment and a fictional equipment purchase and compare where each lands.
perspectives.troubleshooting: If a large cost never appears in cost per litre, check whether its item is one of the three exclusions.

items.title: How expenses are attributed to a period
items.question: How are expenses attributed to a cost period?
alternatives: which period does a cost belong to
why is a cost spread out
items.answer: Each eligible expense carries one of four rules. Direct costs land on their service date, periodic and allocated costs spread across their coverage dates, and consumption costs are counted only as they are actually used.
items.explanation: Direct applies to a cost tied to a single dated event, such as a pregnancy diagnosis or a vet consultation. Periodic applies to costs that cover a span, such as wages, rent, insurance and electricity, and spreads them pro rata across that span. Allocated applies to consumables bought in bulk and drawn down over time, such as teat dip, bedding or antibiotics. Consumption is the narrowest rule and currently governs exactly one item, Semen Straws, which is counted as straws are actually drawn from the linked lot rather than when the batch was purchased. Three items have no automatic method and require the operator to choose: tractor diesel and servicing, farm vehicle fuel and maintenance, and water pumping and borehole maintenance, because each may serve either milk production or other farm activity.

scenario.given: A fictional farm buys a batch of semen straws in January and uses some in February.
steps: Identify the source transaction and the service or coverage period.
Apply the documented attribution rule.
Reconcile allocated totals back to the source amount.
Review the cost result and its explanation.
scenario.expected: Under the consumption rule, the January purchase does not land wholly in January. Straws are counted into the period in which each insemination actually draws one from the lot.
scenario.next: Resolve any unattributed item before relying on the result for a management decision.

persisted: the attribution method where the operator must choose it
derived: the amount attributed to each period
audit: attributed and unattributed amounts both visible

exceptions.condition: The item is tractor diesel, farm vehicle fuel or water pumping.
exceptions.behaviour: No method is applied automatically. The operator chooses, because the cost may or may not serve milk production.

exceptions.condition: The item is classified Non-OPEX.
exceptions.behaviour: No attribution method applies at all, because the cost never reaches operating cost.

exceptions.condition: An amount cannot be attributed.
exceptions.behaviour: It is reported as unattributed rather than dropped or absorbed silently.

items.correction_path: Amend the transaction's method or dates through the governed path; attribution recomputes for the affected periods.
items.safety: Do not double-count an expense across periods, and do not omit one silently. Both are visible by design.

perspectives.operator: A bulk purchase is not necessarily a cost of the month you bought it in.
perspectives.supervisor: The three items with no automatic method need a consistent farm rule.
perspectives.finance: Four methods exist: direct, periodic, allocated and consumption.
perspectives.veterinary_health: Semen straws count as they are used, which ties breeding cost to actual inseminations.
perspectives.technical: CONSUMPTION_ITEMS currently contains only Semen Straws; the semen lot links the purchase to its usage.
perspectives.training: Attribute a fictional annual insurance premium and a fictional semen batch, and compare.
perspectives.troubleshooting: If a period's cost looks wrong, check the attribution method before the amount.

items.title: Cost of production per litre
items.question: How is cost of production per litre calculated?
alternatives: how much does it cost to produce a litre
items.answer: Cost of production per litre is feed cost per litre plus attributed OPEX per litre, over the same selected period and the same milk denominator, with exclusions and unavailable inputs shown rather than hidden.
items.explanation: The two components come from different places on purpose. Feed cost comes from the daily TMR snapshot, not from feed purchase transactions, so buying feed does not itself move cost of production; feeding it does. Attributed OPEX comes from Finance, after the three Non-OPEX exclusions and each item's attribution rule have been applied. Both are divided by the same milk denominator for the same period, which is why an incomplete milk day inside the period understates the denominator and overstates the result. The figure is explainable rather than final: it is not an accounting close, and it moves when a late milk entry, a void or a correction lands inside the period.

scenario.given: A fictional herd produced 1,000 L in a period, with attributable feed cost of PKR 45,000 and attributed OPEX of PKR 20,000.
steps: Confirm the period and its completed-date boundary.
Review the milk litres, the daily TMR costs and the attributed OPEX.
Check excluded and unattributed costs.
Reconcile the displayed total against its components.
scenario.expected: Feed cost per litre is PKR 45. OPEX per litre is PKR 20. Cost of production per litre is PKR 65. Any equipment purchase in the period is excluded and does not appear in either component.
scenario.next: Use the component breakdown to investigate any discrepancy.

audit: traceable to the milk ledger, the TMR snapshots and the attributed transactions

exceptions.condition: The period contains no milk.
exceptions.behaviour: There is no denominator, so a per-litre figure cannot be formed. The inputs are shown rather than a misleading result.

exceptions.condition: A milk day inside the period is incomplete.
exceptions.behaviour: The denominator is understated and cost per litre correspondingly overstated.

exceptions.condition: A cost could not be attributed.
exceptions.behaviour: It is reported as unattributed and excluded from the figure rather than silently absorbed.

items.correction_path: Correct the source milk records, TMR snapshots or transactions. The figure recomputes; it is never edited directly.
items.safety: Do not treat this as a closed accounting figure. It is an explainable management estimate that moves when its inputs are corrected.

perspectives.operator: Buying feed does not change cost per litre. Feeding it does.
perspectives.supervisor: Check milk completeness before comparing one period's cost per litre with another's.
perspectives.finance: Feed cost comes from the daily TMR snapshot; OPEX comes from attributed Finance transactions.
perspectives.veterinary_health: Veterinary costs are operating costs and do contribute.
perspectives.technical: The period total is computed in the integrated cost route, whose source text is pinned by tests.
perspectives.training: Work the 1,000 L example above, then add an incomplete day and watch the figure rise.
perspectives.troubleshooting: An unexpectedly high cost per litre is most often an understated denominator, not an overstated cost.
